notable_claims: ACS employees were reportedly instructed not to discuss the Brack case on the net.
There is a dispute over whether ACS has the authority to ban users from departmental subnetworks or university library systems.
classification.summary: Steve Romig discusses a dispute involving a student named Mr. Brack and the Academic Computing Services (ACS) at Ohio State University. The discussion centers on whether ACS has the authority to ban a user from all university networks, including library systems and departmental machines. Romig cautions against making judgments without hearing the administration's side of the case.

notable_claims: Tolerance for extreme speech on networks is a test of the breadth of freedom.
Mainframe owners should not be held responsible as publishers for content produced by users, or they will inevitably censor it.
The lack of free and easy access to networks risks creating 'information elites' and 'information haves and have-nots'.
Regulation of computer communication via the U.S. Supreme Court is likely inevitable without legislative intervention.
classification.summary: Dean Gottehrer argues that the protection of extreme speech is essential to maintaining freedom and democracy on computer networks. He discusses the legal risks of mainframe owners being held responsible for user content, advocating instead for a common carrier or public forum model. Additionally, he addresses the 'digital divide,' citing Alaska's legislative information system as a model for providing free public access to prevent the rise of information elites.
classification.title: Freedom of communication

notable_claims: Laurence Tribe proposed a constitutional amendment to make free speech and privacy protections applicable regardless of the technological medium.
The proposed amendment would clarify whether users are free to say what they want on state university computers tied into the network.
The author suggests that courts, rather than Congress, are more likely to establish digital rights through case law.
classification.summary: Dean Gottehrer discusses a proposed 27th Amendment by Laurence Tribe intended to ensure constitutional protections apply regardless of the technological medium used. Gottehrer argues that such an amendment would explicitly protect free speech and prevent unreasonable searches on computers at state universities. He also provides a legal context for the right to privacy as it relates to government intrusion.
classification.title: 27th Amendment

notable_claims: The author successfully filed a 19-count grievance for harassment, including the monitoring of private email and files.
University administration often defaults to believing system administrators over students due to perceived technical authority.
Lack of an ombudsman or clear conduct policy can leave students without viable paths for recourse against IT staff.
classification.summary: Helen O'Boyle describes her struggle to find administrative recourse after being targeted by a system administrator at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) in the mid-1980s. She details the failure of university hierarchies, the lack of an ombudsman, and the eventual success of a formal grievance based on harassment and monitoring of private email. The post argues for equal effort requirements for both sysadmins and students when challenging actions to prevent bureaucratic abuse.
classification.title: User recourse (LONG) (was: Ohio State)

notable_claims: Censorship regarding pornography is a primary obstacle to uniform network access in K-12 education.
US government employees allegedly threatened non-CONUS archive sites with disconnection from the Global Internet to force the removal of adult content.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the tension between network censorship and academic freedom, specifically concerning pornography on government-funded networks. The text highlights how sensationalist media reporting on 'pornographic filth' may drive K-12 censorship and threaten uniform network access. It further discusses allegations that US government agencies pressured non-US archive sites to remove content under threat of disconnection.
classification.title: say it aint so, joe
